tools.title: Normal Curve: Areas, z-Scores and Percentiles
tools.intro: Shade any region under a Normal curve and see its area, the z-scores of the cutoffs and the same area on the standard Normal curve. Then work backward from an area to a percentile.
tools.description: Choose a Normal model, shade X < a, X > a, a < X < b or both tails, and read the z-scores and the area (exact and with Table A). Switch to inverse mode to find a percentile from an area, and see the same area on the standard Normal curve.
tools.discovery: The area under a Normal curve depends only on how many standard deviations a cutoff is from the mean: P(X < a) = P(Z < (a − μ)/σ). Table A gives left-tail areas; right tails and intervals come from subtraction, and percentiles come from reading the table backward.

tools.title: Chi-Square: Observed vs Expected
tools.intro: Change observed counts and watch the expected counts, each piece of χ², the total and the p-value. Compare a goodness-of-fit test with a test for independence in a two-way table.
tools.description: Set observed counts for a goodness-of-fit test (four categories against a claimed distribution) or a 2 × 3 two-way table, and see the expected counts, every (O − E)²/E piece, χ², df and the p-value shaded on the chi-square curve. Check the expected-count condition as you go.
tools.discovery: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E measures how far the counts are from what the claim or independence predicts. Larger χ² gives a smaller p-value; with the same proportions, doubling every count doubles χ², so bigger samples give stronger evidence.
